title: Comparatives and superlatives
tagline: Small, smaller, the smallest: how to compare people, places and things.
why: You compare things all day: which bag is heavier, which exercise is easier, who is the tallest in the class. In Speaking Part 2 you compare photos, and in Reading Part 5 the exam checks whether you know bigger from more big. One small mistake here is one of the most common errors at this level.

hook.text: It's Geography class. Miss Vega shows two photos: Lima and Cusco. "Which city is bigger?" she asks. Sofia says, "Lima is bigger, but Cusco is higher!" Mateo laughs: "And it's definitely colder in the mountains!"
hook.ask: Bigger, higher and colder all compare two things. Can you see the small change at the end of each short word?

items.label: Mateo's dog is the biggest of the three.

diagrams.title: Spelling: -er and -est

rules.rule: Ends in -e: just add r / st
One vowel + one consonant: double the consonant

diagrams.caption: Say the adjective out loud first, then add the ending — your ear usually knows the spelling.

rows.label: Rule
cells: put more / the most in front

examples.text: This book is more interesting than that film.
Cusco is colder than Lima in July.

use.point: Superlatives: the best in the whole group

examples.text: Huascarán is the highest mountain in Peru.
examples.note: one thing out of a group → the + -est

examples.text: This is the most difficult question in the test.
Nadia is the youngest student in our class.
examples.note: comparing a person to the whole group

examples.text: The weather today is better than yesterday.
examples.note: good → better → the best, no -er here

examples.text: My grades this term are worse than last term.
Arequipa is further from Lima than Ica.

use.point: as…as, not as…as and much + comparative

examples.text: This exercise isn't as easy as the last one.
examples.note: negative form shows there's a difference
much/a lot before the comparative for extra emphasis

watch_out.wrong: This city is more big than Lima.
My phone is more good than yours.
watch_out.why: Good has its own comparative: better, never more good.

watch_out.wrong: Lima is as big than Arequipa.
watch_out.why: as…as needs as on both sides, never as…than.

watch_out.wrong: He is the tallest boy of the class.
watch_out.right: He is the tallest boy in the class.
watch_out.why: With a group of people, English uses in, not of.

l1.es: Es más grande que mi casa.
l1.wrong: It's more big than my house.
l1.why: Spanish always says más + adjective, but English changes short adjectives to -er instead of using more.

l1.es: Es el chico más alto de la clase.
l1.wrong: He's the tallest boy of the class.
l1.right: He's the tallest boy in the class.
l1.why: Spanish de becomes in with a group in English, not of.

l1.es: Es tan alto como su hermano.
l1.wrong: He is so tall as his brother.
l1.why: The Spanish tan…como pattern is as…as in English, not so…as.

l1.es: Es el mejor jugador del equipo.
l1.wrong: He's the goodest player of the team.
l1.right: He's the best player in the team.
l1.why: Good has no -est form: it becomes best, and groups use in.

remember.tip: Count the syllables in your head: one → add -er or -est. Two or more → put more or the most in front instead.

dialogue.title: Cusco or Lima?
dialogue.context: In Geography class, Miss Vega asks the students to compare two Peruvian cities for a project.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: For your project, compare Cusco and Lima. Which city is bigger?

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: Lima is much bigger than Cusco. It's the biggest city in Peru!

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: But Cusco is higher than Lima — it's up in the mountains.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: Yes! In June, Cusco is colder, but Lima is more humid.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: I think Cusco is the most beautiful city in Peru, with all those old streets.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Good point. Is it as busy as Lima?

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: No, it isn't as busy as Lima. Lima has the most traffic of any city I know!

can_do: I can compare two things using -er, more and than.
I can say which thing is the biggest, the best or the most interesting with superlatives.
I can use as…as to say two things are equal.
summary: Short adjectives (one syllable) add -er and the + -est: small → smaller → the smallest.
Long adjectives (two or more syllables) use more and the most: interesting → more interesting → the most interesting.
Some adjectives are irregular: good → better → the best, bad → worse → the worst, far → further → the furthest.
Use as…as to say two things are equal, and than after any comparative.
